faq.a: Consider ventricular tachycardia; assess haemodynamic stability and prepare for immediate cardioversion if unstable.
faq.q: What is the first step when an ECG shows a wide QRS and a regular rapid rhythm?

faq.a: Severe anaemia and fever may cause sinus tachycardia; high parasitaemia can lead to myocarditis with diffuse ST changes.
faq.q: How can malaria affect the ECG?

faq.a: Many antimalarials (e.g., quinine) lengthen QT; combined with electrolyte loss they raise torsades risk.
faq.q: Why is QT prolongation dangerous in patients on antimalarials?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with palpitations – what ECG features confirm atrial enlargement and how does this affect management? — Look for P‑wave >120 ms in lead II and biphasic P in V1; anticoagulate if atrial fibrillation develops.

You receive an ECG with ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF in a patient with chest pain – what is your next immediate action? — Give aspirin, arrange for reperfusion (thrombolysis if PCI unavailable), monitor for arrhythmia.
A patient on quinine for severe malaria develops a QTc of 520 ms – what should you do? — Stop quinine, give IV magnesium, correct electrolytes, avoid other QT‑prolonging drugs.

An ECG shows a regular rhythm at 180 bpm with narrow QRS complexes – what is the most likely diagnosis and first treatment? — Supraventricular tachycardia; attempt vagal manoeuvres, then IV adenosine if stable.

A newborn in a rural clinic has a heart rate of 45 bpm and a complete AV block on ECG – what is the urgent management? — Give atropine, prepare for temporary pacing if possible, arrange transfer to higher‑level centre.
How does chronic hypertension alter the ECG and what does it predict? — Leads to left ventricular hypertrophy (Sokolow‑Lyon criteria); predicts future heart failure and arrhythmia risk.

A patient with HIV presents with low voltage QRS and pericardial rub – what ECG finding supports pericarditis and what is the treatment? — Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression; give NSAIDs and treat underlying infection.

Why might a patient with severe diarrhoea have a normal ECG despite feeling faint? — Electrolyte loss (especially K+) can cause subtle changes; treat dehydration and replace electrolytes, repeat ECG after correction.
ai.title: ECG Interpretation for Clinicians
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A practical guide to interpreting a 12‑lead ECG at the bedside, focusing on common tropical diseases and low‑resource settings. It links patterns to pathophysiology, urgent red flags and management without relying on advanced testing.

b: Standard 12‑lead placement (limb leads I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF; precordial V1‑V6)
Normal sinus rhythm: rate 60‑100 bpm, PR 120‑200 ms, QRS <120 ms, QTc <440 ms (men) / <460 ms (women)
sections.p: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity via surface electrodes, producing a 12‑lead tracing that reflects atrial and ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation.

b: Ischaemic heart disease (often silent, linked to hypertension, diabetes, tobacco)
Rheumatic heart disease with atrial enlargement
Malaria‑related anaemia causing tachycardia
HIV‑associated cardiomyopathy
Electrolyte disturbances from diarrhoea or renal disease
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, the most frequent ECG abnormalities stem from:

b: Chest pain → look for ST‑segment changes
Palpitations → assess rhythm disturbances
Syncope → evaluate for high‑grade AV block or ventricular tachycardia
sections.p: Patients may present with chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations or syncope, but many are asymptomatic and the ECG is the first clue.

t.b: What is the cardiac rhythm and are there ischaemic or conduction abnormalities? – Identifies arrhythmias, ST‑segment deviation, QRS widening, QT prolongation.
Do electrolyte disturbances explain arrhythmia? – Low K+ (<3.5 mmol/L) or Mg2+ (<0.7 mmol/L) can cause torsades or PVCs.
Is there myocardial injury? – Elevated troponin with ST elevation confirms MI.
Is there pulmonary congestion or pneumothorax that could mimic ECG changes? – Helps differentiate left‑sided strain from primary cardiac cause.

b: ST‑segment elevation >1 mm in two contiguous leads – acute MI, needs urgent reperfusion
New‑onset complete heart block – risk of asystole
Wide QRS (>120 ms) with ventricular rate >150 bpm – possible ventricular tachycardia
QTc >500 ms – risk of torsades de pointes
sections.p: Certain ECG patterns predict imminent deterioration.

b: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response: rate control with beta‑blocker (e.g., metoprolol) unless contraindicated; consider digoxin if beta‑blocker unavailable.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then stabilise the rhythm and support perfusion.

b: Post‑MI: schedule stress ECG or echocardiography when feasible.
Rheumatic disease: secondary prophylaxis with penicillin to prevent recurrence.
Hypertension and diabetes control to reduce future ischaemic changes.
sections.p: Repeat ECG after acute management to confirm resolution and guide long‑term therapy.

b: Pericarditis – diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, not localized to coronary territories.
Early repolarisation – benign ST elevation in V2‑V5, seen in young healthy individuals.
Left bundle‑branch block – wide QRS with secondary ST‑T changes, can mask MI.
sections.p: Conditions that can mimic ECG findings.

b: Hyperkalaemia may produce peaked T waves that resemble acute MI ST changes.
Low voltage QRS in obesity or COPD can hide pathological Q waves.
Artifact from movement or poor electrode contact can mimic arrhythmia.

whenToSeekHelp: Syncope with new complete heart block
